subject: Discovery recap: function orchestration acceptance criteria & next steps
messages:
From: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwoodinference.com>
To: Alex Silva <alex.silva@paylance.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwoodinference.com>, Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwoodinference.com>
Date: 2026-10-22T15:03:00-07:00
Subject: Discovery recap: function orchestration acceptance criteria & next steps

Alex — thanks again for the time today. Quick recap from our call so we have shared alignment and clear next steps. I kept this intentionally concise.

What we heard (pain points)
- Downstream parsing failures: your existing rule-based consumers break frequently because model outputs are freeform and occasionally include unexpected fields/type changes.
- Orchestration opacity: current function chain (Airflow + custom microservices) struggles to validate outputs between steps, making retries/debugging expensive.
- Cost & SLOs: you need predictable latency for the customer-facing flows (interactive payments verification) and a path to reduce token costs for high-throughput batch jobs.

Current stack (from call)
- Ingress: frontend -> payments gateway -> orchestration layer (Airflow) -> microservices
- Models: mix of hosted LLM APIs + homegrown heuristics for post-processing
- Observability: limited tracing between model call -> function execution -> downstream system

Success criteria (what PayLance wants to validate)
1) Deterministic structured outputs: responses must validate against a stable JSON schema (no silent/incompatible changes).
2) Explicit tool/function-call traces: each model output must include which internal tools were invoked and with what parameters (for audit + replay).
3) Validation & fallback policies: automatic reject/repair path for invalid outputs and safe default behavior for payment-critical steps.
4) Performance windows: median inference <250ms for interactive checks; 95th percentile under 1s for typical payment flows (we'll vet exact SLOs in the tech deep dive).
5) Lightweight acceptance tests: a small set of deterministic prompts + expected schema outputs for continuous quality checks.

Redwood approach (summary)
- Function/Tool calling + JSON-schema handshake to make outputs enforceable.
- Agent workflows with explicit step metadata (tool name, version, inputs/outputs) so you can replay and audit.
- Optimize profiles (batching + quantization) for your high-throughput jobs to hit cost targets without sacrificing schema stability.

Suggested next steps
1) I attached a starter schema (paylance-sample-schema-v1.json) that captures the core payment-verification output we sketched. Please review and flag missing fields.
2) Tech deep dive (60 min) with your engineering team: proposed slots Tue 2026-10-27 10:00–11:00 PT or Wed 2026-10-28 14:00–15:00 PT. Monica and Ben will join to walk the runtime and validation options.
3) You send a small sample of failing examples (CSV) so we can build acceptance tests (we offered to convert to test vectors).
4) We will prepare a short PoC plan that covers schema enforcement, a sample function pipeline, and acceptance tests.

Attachments: paylance-sample-schema-v1.json (starter), acceptance-tests.csv (template), recording stub (rdw-discovery-recording.mp4).

If that all looks right, pick a deep-dive slot and we'll lock it. Thanks — looking forward to tackling the flaky parsing and getting you a deterministic pipeline.

—
Neha Kapoor

From: Alex Silva <alex.silva@paylance.com>

Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwoodinference.com>, Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwoodinference.com>
Date: 2026-10-22T17:30:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Discovery recap: function orchestration acceptance criteria & next steps

Thanks Neha — helpful summary. A few clarifications from our side: 

- Priority: making the payment-verification outputs machine-parseable is the highest priority. If we can guarantee schema stability for the verification step, the rest of the pipeline becomes much simpler.
- Nested arrays: we have a use case where an event can include multiple instrument checks (array of objects) and those arrays must preserve ordering and contain a deterministic id per instrument — can your starter schema show an example nested array?
- Cost ballpark: can you give a rough cost-per-100k-transactions estimate for the dedicated vs hosted approach so we know whether to push for Dedicated early? A high-level number is fine for now.

We can confirm Tue 2026-10-27 10:00 PT for the deep dive — adding our payments engineering lead (Carlos) to the meeting invite.

Also: I attached one anonymized failure sample in the CSV; it shows the output that breaks our parser (freeform reason text). We'll upload the full set into the shared doc.

Appreciate the clear path forward.

—Alex
Alex Silva
Head of Integrations, PayLance
alex.silva@paylance.com
From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwoodinference.com>
To: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwoodinference.com>, Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwoodinference.com>
Date: 2026-10-23T09:04:00-07:00
Subject: Internal: prep for PayLance deep dive (schema + validation kit)

Quick internal note — capturing action items before the deep dive on Tue: 

1) Expand the starter schema to include a nested array example and explicit 'instrument_id' with stable UUID format. File: paylance-sample-schema-v1.json -> v1.1 for the deep dive.
2) Build a lightweight validation harness: a small Python script that rejects non-conforming outputs and returns canonical repair suggestions (useful as demo).
3) Prepare acceptance-tests.csv from the sample they sent; include 8 deterministic prompts that exercise edge-cases (missing fields / extra fields / array ordering).
4) Cost estimates: draft back-of-envelope for hosted vs Dedicated for 100k tx/month and 1M tx/month. Include token estimates with typical inference profile.

Monica — can you own the validation harness and demo pipeline? I can own the cost write-up and example rollback policy (automatic fallback to a safe microservice response).

Thanks — Ben
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
